chapters.title: Household Water Readiness
chapters.summary: Practical local routines for storing, rotating, and using household water more safely when normal service is disrupted.

sections.heading: Store And Label Water By Household Use
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Separate drinking water from utility water before you need either.

- Keep the cleanest containers dedicated to drinking and food prep.
- Label containers with fill date and intended use.
- Store them where temperature swings and chemical exposure stay low.
- Keep a smaller grab-fast set near the path you would actually leave with.

A smaller well-labeled water plan is more usable than a large mixed stash nobody trusts under stress.

sections.heading: Boil-Water Notice Routine
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Treat a boil-water notice as a kitchen workflow change, not just a stove task.

- Set aside one clean area for treated water containers only.
- Use a pot, kettle, or device you already know how to run safely.
- Cool treated water in covered containers before putting it into regular household rotation.
- Keep untreated water and treated water physically separated so nobody guesses wrong.

If you cannot keep treatment and storage steps straight, use bottled or otherwise known-safe water until the routine is simpler.

sections.heading: Low-Water Sanitation Fallback
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Save your cleanest water for drinking first, then set a clear minimum hygiene routine.

- Keep one hand-cleaning station and one dish or wipe-down station instead of spreading water everywhere.
- Use soap and friction first whenever possible.
- Move laundry, deep cleaning, and noncritical rinsing later if water is limited.
- Track what counts as utility water so it does not drift back into drinking use.

Under stress, simple sanitation lanes reduce waste and prevent avoidable cross-contamination.

sections.heading: Quarterly Water Rotation Loop
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Water readiness stays useful when it lives on a calendar.

- Check labels and oldest dates first.
- Rotate small containers before deep storage you rarely touch.
- Inspect seals, odors, cloudiness, and storage locations before refilling.
- Update the inventory record the same day so the list and the shelf still match.

Short frequent checks beat occasional full resets that leave old containers forgotten in the back.
